records.source: וַיְהִי֩ אִ֨ישׁ אֶחָ֜ד מִן־הָרָמָתַ֛יִם צוֹפִ֖ים מֵהַ֣ר אֶפְרָ֑יִם וּשְׁמ֡וֹ אֶ֠לְקָנָה בֶּן־יְרֹחָ֧ם בֶּן־אֱלִיה֛וּא בֶּן־תֹּ֥חוּ בֶן־צ֖וּף אֶפְרָתִֽי׃
records.gloss: And there was a man, one, from Ramathaim-zophim, from [the] hill country of Ephraim, and his name [was] Elkanah, son of Jeroham, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, an Ephraimite.
pieces: There was a man from Ramathaim-zophim in the hill country of Ephraim named Elkanah son of Jeroham, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, an Ephraimite.

L.1: And there was a certain man from Ramathaim-zophim, from the hill country of Ephraim, and his name [was] Elkanah son of Jeroham, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, an Ephraimite.

R.1: There was a man named Elkanah who lived in the town of Ramathaim-zophim, in the hills of Ephraim. His father was Jeroham, and his family line went back through Elihu and Tohu to Zuph. He was from Ephraim.

decisions.choice: the setting: the last days of the judges, before Israel had a king
decisions.reason: The book opens where Judges leaves off. Israel has no king (Judges 21:25), and Eli the priest has led Israel from the sanctuary at Shiloh (verses 3 and 9; 4:18). The story of Samuel, the last of the judges (7:15), who will anoint Israel's first two kings (10:1; 16:13), begins with one ordinary family in the hills of Ephraim. 1 and 2 Samuel were a single book in the Hebrew Bible; the division into two comes from the ancient Greek translation.

decisions.choice: There was a certain man from ...: the opening of Judges 13 and 17
decisions.reason: The words echo the start of Samson's story, "There was a certain man from Zorah ... and his name was Manoah" (Judges 13:2), and of Micah's (Judges 17:1). As in Samson's story, a wife who cannot have children and a son given by God follow (verse 2).

decisions.choice: Ramathaim-zophim: "the two heights" of the Zuphites, the town called Ramah in verse 19
decisions.reason: Ramathaim means "two heights". Elsewhere the town is simply Ramah, "the height" (verse 19; 2:11), and it is Samuel's home all his life (7:17). Zophim seems to point to the family of Zuph, named at the end of the verse; the area is called "the land of Zuph" in 9:5. The letters can also be divided to read "Ramathaim, a Zuphite", describing Elkanah; the sense is much the same.

decisions.choice: Ephraimite: a man of the hill country of Ephraim
decisions.reason: The word can also mean someone from Ephrathah, the clan around Bethlehem (Ruth 1:2; 1 Samuel 17:12), but the hill country of Ephraim in this verse decides the sense here, as in Judges 12:5 and 1 Kings 11:26. It says where the family lived. 1 Chronicles 6 lists Elkanah and Samuel among the descendants of Levi, a tribe that had towns within Ephraim (Joshua 21:20-22).

decisions.choice: the town of ...; his family line went back through ... to Zuph
decisions.reason: Readable says that Ramathaim-zophim is a town and turns the list of ancestors into a sentence of its own.

records.heading: Hannah asks {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} for a son

records.source: וְלוֹ֙ שְׁתֵּ֣י נָשִׁ֔ים שֵׁ֤ם אַחַת֙ חַנָּ֔ה וְשֵׁ֥ם הַשֵּׁנִ֖ית פְּנִנָּ֑ה וַיְהִ֤י לִפְנִנָּה֙ יְלָדִ֔ים וּלְחַנָּ֖ה אֵ֥ין יְלָדִֽים׃
records.gloss: And to him [were] two wives; [the] name of one [was] Hannah, and [the] name of the second [was] Peninnah. And there were to Peninnah children, and to Hannah there were no children.
pieces: He had two wives. One was named Hannah and the other Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah had none.

L.2: And he had two wives: the name of one [was] Hannah, and the name of the second [was] Peninnah. And Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children.

R.2: Elkanah had two wives, Hannah and Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah did not have any.

decisions.choice: two wives: a home with a rival wife
decisions.reason: The law allowed a man more than one wife (Deuteronomy 21:15-17), but Scripture's stories of such homes are stories of rivalry: Sarah and Hagar (Genesis 16), Rachel and Leah (Genesis 29:31-30:24). Peninnah will be called Hannah's rival (verse 6).

decisions.choice: Hannah had no children: a deep grief and a shame
decisions.reason: A wife without children was often pitied or looked down on (Genesis 16:4; 30:1, 23). Hannah joins the women of Scripture who could not have children until God gave them a son: Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and the wife of Manoah (Genesis 11:30; 25:21; 29:31; Judges 13:2).

decisions.choice: Hannah: "grace" or "favor"; Peninnah: perhaps "pearl" or "coral"
decisions.reason: Hannah's name comes from the word for grace or favor. Peninnah's is less certain; it may come from a word for a precious stone, pearl or coral. The story does not make anything of either meaning.

decisions.choice: the second: the other wife
decisions.reason: The word means "second". It may simply mean "the other one", or that Elkanah married Peninnah after Hannah. The text does not say why he took a second wife.

decisions.choice: Elkanah had two wives
decisions.reason: Readable names Elkanah for "he" and gives the two names in one sentence.

records.source: וְעָלָה֩ הָאִ֨ישׁ הַה֤וּא מֵֽעִירוֹ֙ מִיָּמִ֣ים׀יָמִ֔ימָה לְהִֽשְׁתַּחֲוֺ֧ת וְלִזְבֹּ֛חַ לַיהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת בְּשִׁלֹ֑ה וְשָׁ֞ם שְׁנֵ֣י בְנֵֽי־עֵלִ֗י חָפְנִי֙ וּפִ֣נְחָ֔ס כֹּהֲנִ֖ים לַיהוָֽה׃
records.gloss: And went up the man, that [one], from his city from days to days to bow down and to sacrifice to Yahweh of hosts in Shiloh; and there [were the] two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, priests to Yahweh.
pieces: Year after year this man went up from his town to worship and to offer sacrifice to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies at Shiloh. The two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were priests of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} there.

L.3: And that man went up from his city year by year to worship and to sacrifice to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of hosts in Shiloh; and there the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, [were] priests of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

R.3: Every year Elkanah left his town and went up to Shiloh to worship {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies and to offer sacrifices to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. Eli's two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, served as priests of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} there.

decisions.choice: Yahweh of hosts: Yahweh, commander of the armies of heaven and earth
decisions.reason: This is the first time the title appears in the Bible. Tseba'ot is the plural of tsava', an army or host, a great company drawn up in ranks. The word is used of Israel's armies (Exodus 12:41; 1 Samuel 17:45), of the sun, moon and stars (Genesis 2:1; Deuteronomy 4:19) and of the heavenly beings around God's throne (1 Kings 22:19). Joined to God's name, it presents Yahweh as the King who commands every power in heaven and on earth. In 1 Samuel the title is tied to the ark kept at Shiloh, "the ark of the covenant of Yahweh of hosts, who is enthroned on the cherubim" (4:4), and David goes out against Goliath "in the name of Yahweh of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel" (17:45). Hannah calls on God by this name in her vow (verse 11).

decisions.choice: Shiloh: the place of Israel's central sanctuary
decisions.reason: Shiloh lay in the hill country of Ephraim, north of Bethel (Judges 21:19). The tent of meeting had been set up there in Joshua's day (Joshua 18:1), and the ark of the covenant was kept there (3:3; 4:3-4). Israelites went up to it for a yearly feast (Judges 21:19).

decisions.choice: from days to days: year by year
decisions.reason: "Days" here stands for a full year, as in Exodus 13:10 and Judges 11:40; 21:19. The visit was a yearly one (verses 7 and 21), perhaps at one of the great feasts.

decisions.choice: Hophni and Phinehas: Eli's sons, the priests at Shiloh
decisions.reason: Eli was the chief priest (verse 9), and his sons served with him. The writer names them here because of what follows: they will treat Yahweh's offerings with contempt (2:12-17), and both will die on one day, as a sign against Eli's house (2:34; 4:11). Phinehas bears the name of Aaron's faithful grandson (Numbers 25:7-13).

decisions.choice: the LORD of Armies
decisions.reason: "Hosts" was once the ordinary word for an army, but today it most often means someone who welcomes guests, so it hides what the title says. Balanced and Readable say "Armies", as in Isaiah and throughout Samuel and Kings: it states the meaning plainly and keeps the picture of a commander. "Almighty" was considered, but it turns the picture into an abstract quality. Literal keeps the traditional "the LORD of hosts".

decisions.choice: Year after year this man (Balanced); Every year Elkanah (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the time first, and Readable names Elkanah for "that man" and says that the sacrifices were offered to the LORD.

records.source: וַיְהִ֣י הַיּ֔וֹם וַיִּזְבַּ֖ח אֶלְקָנָ֑ה וְנָתַ֞ן לִפְנִנָּ֣ה אִשְׁתּ֗וֹ וּֽלְכָל־בָּנֶ֛יהָ וּבְנוֹתֶ֖יהָ מָנֽוֹת׃
records.gloss: And it was the day, and sacrificed Elkanah, and he gave to Peninnah his wife and to all her sons and her daughters portions.
pieces: On the day Elkanah offered his sacrifice, he would give portions of the meat to his wife Peninnah and to all her sons and daughters.

L.4: And [when] the day came [that] Elkanah sacrificed, he would give portions to Peninnah his wife and to all her sons and her daughters.

R.4: Each year, on the day Elkanah offered his sacrifice, he gave shares of the meat to his wife Peninnah and to each of her sons and daughters.

decisions.choice: sacrificed ... portions: the shared meal of a sacrifice
decisions.reason: The verb is used of the sacrifice whose meat the worshipers ate together before Yahweh, after the fat was burned on the altar and the priest had his share (Leviticus 3; 7:11-18, 31-34; Deuteronomy 12:17-18). The head of the family shared out the meat; a portion was one person's share of food at a meal (9:23).

decisions.choice: and it was the day ... he would give: what happened every year
decisions.reason: The opening words and the verb forms that follow describe the custom of each yearly visit (verse 7), not one particular day. The story turns to a single visit in verse 9.

decisions.choice: portions of the meat (Balanced); Each year ... shares of the meat (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the portions were, and Readable adds "Each year" to show that this was a custom (m2).

records.source: וּלְחַנָּ֕ה יִתֵּ֛ן מָנָ֥ה אַחַ֖ת אַפָּ֑יִם כִּ֤י אֶת־חַנָּה֙ אָהֵ֔ב וַֽיהוָ֖ה סָגַ֥ר רַחְמָֽהּ׃
records.gloss: And to Hannah he gave portion one, of two faces, for Hannah he loved, and Yahweh had closed her womb.
pieces: But to Hannah he gave a double portion, because he loved her, even though {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had closed her womb.

L.5: But to Hannah he would give one double portion, for he loved Hannah, though {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had closed her womb.

R.5: But he gave Hannah twice as much, because he loved her, even though {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had not let her have children.

decisions.choice: a double portion: a share twice the usual size
alternatives: only one portion, though he loved her
a special portion, a portion of honor
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "one portion of two faces" (or "of two nostrils"), an expression found only here. It is often read as "a double portion", which fits the reason that follows: he loved her. Others take the word "face" in the sense of sadness or of honor: "only one portion, sadly", since she had no children to share it with, or "a portion of honor". The ancient Greek translation reads "one portion, because she had no child; yet Elkanah loved Hannah more than Peninnah".

decisions.choice: for he loved Hannah, though Yahweh had closed her womb: two facts set side by side
decisions.reason: Both clauses put their subject or object first, which sets them against each other: Elkanah's love was real, but it could not give Hannah a child.

decisions.choice: Yahweh had closed her womb: her barrenness is in God's hands
decisions.reason: The narrator says twice (verses 5 and 6) that Yahweh closed Hannah's womb. Scripture speaks of God closing and opening the womb (Genesis 20:18; 29:31; 30:22), so the one who closed it is the one Hannah must ask (verse 11), and the son, when he comes, is God's gift (verses 19-20).

decisions.choice: twice as much; had not let her have children
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what a double portion and a closed womb mean.

records.source: וְכִֽעֲסַ֤תָּה צָֽרָתָהּ֙ גַּם־כַּ֔עַס בַּעֲב֖וּר הַרְּעִמָ֑הּ כִּֽי־סָגַ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה בְּעַ֥ד רַחְמָֽהּ׃
records.gloss: And provoked her her rival, also provocation, in order to make her fret, for had closed Yahweh behind her womb.
pieces: Her rival kept taunting her bitterly to upset her, because {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had closed her womb.

L.6: And her rival would provoke her, even sorely, in order to make her fret, because {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had shut up her womb.

R.6: Peninnah, her rival, kept teasing her cruelly to make her miserable, because {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had not let her have children.

decisions.choice: rival: a fellow wife
decisions.reason: The word comes from a root meaning to press hard or to be hostile. It is used of a second wife in the same home, who was naturally a rival (Leviticus 18:18 uses the related verb of taking a wife's sister "as a rival"). Peninnah is meant (verses 2 and 4).

decisions.choice: provoke: to stir up grief and anger by taunting
decisions.reason: The verb and its noun mean to vex or provoke. Here the noun follows the verb, which makes it strong: she provoked her greatly. The word runs through the story: Peninnah provoked her year after year (verse 7), and Hannah tells Eli that she has been praying out of her anguish and "provocation" (verse 16).

decisions.choice: make her fret: upset her, stir her up inside
decisions.reason: The verb usually means "to thunder" or "to roar". In this form it is used of stirring a person up inside, making her tremble with distress. It has this sense only here.

decisions.choice: Peninnah, her rival ... had not let her have children
decisions.reason: Readable names Peninnah and says plainly what a closed womb means, as in verse 5.

records.source: וְכֵ֨ן יַעֲשֶׂ֜ה שָׁנָ֣ה בְשָׁנָ֗ה מִדֵּ֤י עֲלֹתָהּ֙ בְּבֵ֣ית יְהוָ֔ה כֵּ֖ן תַּכְעִסֶ֑נָּה וַתִּבְכֶּ֖ה וְלֹ֥א תֹאכַֽל׃
records.gloss: And so he did year by year; as often as her going up to [the] house of Yahweh, so she provoked her, and she wept and did not eat.
pieces: So it went on year after year. Every time Hannah went up to the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, Peninnah provoked her, and she wept and would not eat.

L.7: And so he did year by year; as often as she went up to the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, so she would provoke her, and she would weep and not eat.

R.7: This happened every year. Each time Hannah went up to the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, Peninnah upset her so much that she cried and would not eat.

decisions.choice: so he did year by year: the same scene was repeated every year
alternatives: so she (Peninnah) did year by year
decisions.reason: The verb is "he did", most naturally Elkanah, who went up and shared out the portions every year (verses 3-5). The ancient Greek reads "she did", meaning Peninnah. Either way the point is that the scene of verses 4-6 happened again on every visit.

decisions.choice: the house of Yahweh: the sanctuary at Shiloh
decisions.reason: The sanctuary at Shiloh is called a house (here; 3:15) and a temple (verse 9). It had doorposts and doors (verse 9; 3:15), so by this time it was more than a tent, though 2:22 still speaks of the tent of meeting. "Went up" is the usual word for travel to a sanctuary.

decisions.choice: she wept and would not eat: what happened each time
decisions.reason: The verbs describe the pattern of each visit. Grief took away Hannah's appetite at the very meal that was meant for rejoicing before Yahweh (Deuteronomy 12:7).

decisions.choice: So it went on (Balanced); This happened (Readable); Hannah, Peninnah
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say that the scene was repeated without naming who "did" it (m1), and they name Hannah and Peninnah where the Hebrew has only "she" and "her".

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר לָ֜הּ אֶלְקָנָ֣ה אִישָׁ֗הּ חַנָּה֙ לָ֣מֶה תִבְכִּ֗י וְלָ֨מֶה֙ לֹ֣א תֹֽאכְלִ֔י וְלָ֖מֶה יֵרַ֣ע לְבָבֵ֑ךְ הֲל֤וֹא אָֽנֹכִי֙ ט֣וֹב לָ֔ךְ מֵעֲשָׂרָ֖ה בָּנִֽים׃
records.gloss: And said to her Elkanah her husband, Hannah, why do you weep? And why do you not eat? And why is your heart bad? Am not I better to you than ten sons?
pieces: Her husband Elkanah said to her, "Hannah, why are you crying? Why do you not eat? Why are you so downcast? Do I not mean more to you than ten sons?"

L.8: And Elkanah her husband said to her, "Hannah, why do you weep? And why do you not eat? And why is your heart bad? Am I not better to you than ten sons?"

R.8: Her husband Elkanah asked her, "Hannah, why are you crying? Why will you not eat? Why are you so sad? Am I not worth more to you than ten sons would be?"

decisions.choice: why is your heart bad: why are you so sad
decisions.reason: When the heart is "bad", a person is downcast or grieved (Nehemiah 2:2, where a sad face shows "badness of heart"). It is not a charge of wickedness.

decisions.choice: Am I not better to you than ten sons?: a question that expects yes
decisions.reason: Elkanah means that his love should be enough for her. "Ten" is a round number for a full family; compare Ruth 4:15, where Ruth is "better to you than seven sons". The story does not give Hannah's answer.

decisions.choice: so downcast (Balanced); so sad (Readable)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "your heart bad"; Balanced and Readable give its sense (m1).

records.source: וַתָּ֣קָם חַנָּ֔ה אַחֲרֵ֛י אָכְלָ֥ה בְשִׁלֹ֖ה וְאַחֲרֵ֣י שָׁתֹ֑ה וְעֵלִ֣י הַכֹּהֵ֗ן יֹשֵׁב֙ עַל־הַכִּסֵּ֔א עַל־מְזוּזַ֖ת הֵיכַ֥ל יְהוָֽה׃
records.gloss: And arose Hannah after her eating in Shiloh and after drinking; and Eli the priest [was] sitting on the seat by [the] doorpost of [the] temple of Yahweh.
pieces: Once, when the eating and drinking at Shiloh were over, Hannah got up. Eli the priest sat on his seat beside the doorpost of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}'s temple.

L.9: And Hannah rose after her eating in Shiloh and after drinking. And Eli the priest [was] sitting on the seat by the doorpost of the temple of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

R.9: One year, after the meal at Shiloh was over, Hannah got up. Eli the priest was sitting on his chair beside the doorway of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}'s temple.

decisions.choice: after the eating and drinking at Shiloh: when the meal was over
alternatives: after she had eaten and drunk
decisions.reason: The words are "after her eating in Shiloh and after drinking". They may mean that Hannah had eaten this time, or simply mark the time: when the sacrificial meal was over. Since verse 7 says she would not eat, and verse 18 says she ate after Eli's blessing, the sense is more likely the end of the family's meal. The ancient Greek reads "after they had eaten".

decisions.choice: the seat: a seat of honor
decisions.reason: The word is the usual word for a throne. Eli sits at the entrance of the sanctuary as its chief priest and Israel's leader (4:18), where he can see who comes and goes. He will be sitting on this seat when the news of the ark reaches him, and he will fall from it and die (4:13, 18).

decisions.choice: temple: a great house, a palace
decisions.reason: The word means a palace or a large building and is used of Yahweh's dwelling as the house of a King. Here it names the sanctuary at Shiloh (see verse 7).

decisions.choice: Once (Balanced); One year (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable show that the story now moves from the yearly custom (verses 3-8) to one particular visit.

records.source: וְהִ֖יא מָ֣רַת נָ֑פֶשׁ וַתִּתְפַּלֵּ֥ל עַל־יְהוָ֖ה וּבָכֹ֥ה תִבְכֶּֽה׃
records.gloss: And she [was] bitter of soul, and she prayed to Yahweh, and weeping she wept.
pieces: She was in deep anguish, and she prayed to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, weeping without restraint.

L.10: And she [was] bitter of soul, and she prayed to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and wept and wept.

R.10: Hannah was very sad and upset. She cried and cried as she prayed to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: bitter of soul: in deep anguish
decisions.reason: Bitterness of the nefesh, the inner self, is deep grief or distress (Job 3:20; 2 Kings 4:27, of the woman of Shunem whose son had died). Naomi asked to be called Mara, "bitter", for the same reason (Ruth 1:20).

decisions.choice: weeping she wept: she wept and wept
decisions.reason: The verb is doubled for emphasis, a common Hebrew way of strengthening an action: she wept without stopping.

decisions.choice: in deep anguish, weeping without restraint (Balanced); very sad and upset, cried and cried (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of "bitter of soul" (m1); Readable keeps the doubled verb as "cried and cried".

records.source: וַתִּדֹּ֨ר נֶ֜דֶר וַתֹּאמַ֗ר יְהוָ֨ה צְבָא֜וֹת אִם־רָאֹ֥ה תִרְאֶ֣ה׀בָּעֳנִ֣י אֲמָתֶ֗ךָ וּזְכַרְתַּ֨נִי֙ וְלֹֽא־תִשְׁכַּ֣ח אֶת־אֲמָתֶ֔ךָ וְנָתַתָּ֥ה לַאֲמָתְךָ֖ זֶ֣רַע אֲנָשִׁ֑ים וּנְתַתִּ֤יו לַֽיהוָה֙ כָּל־יְמֵ֣י חַיָּ֔יו וּמוֹרָ֖ה לֹא־יַעֲלֶ֥ה עַל־רֹאשֽׁוֹ׃
records.gloss: And she vowed a vow and said, Yahweh of hosts, if indeed you will look on [the] affliction of your maidservant and remember me and not forget your maidservant and give to your maidservant seed of men, then I will give him to Yahweh all [the] days of his life, and a razor will not go up on his head.
pieces: She made a vow and said, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies, if {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} will only look on the misery of {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} servant and remember me, if {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} will not forget {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} servant but will give {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} servant a son, then I will give him to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} for his whole life, and no razor will ever touch his head."

L.11: And she vowed a vow and said, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} of hosts, if {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} will indeed look on the affliction of {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} maidservant and remember me, and not forget {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} maidservant, but give {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} maidservant a seed of men, then I will give him to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} all the days of his life, and a razor shall not go up on his head."

R.11: She made a solemn promise. She said, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies, I am {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} servant. Please see how I am suffering, and remember me. Do not forget me. If {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} will give me a son, I will give him to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} for his whole life. No razor will ever cut his hair."

decisions.choice: she vowed a vow: a solemn promise to God, made with a request
decisions.reason: A vow promised God a gift if he granted what was asked (Genesis 28:20-22; Numbers 21:2; Judges 11:30-31), and it had to be kept (Deuteronomy 23:22-24). A husband could cancel his wife's vow on the day he heard of it (Numbers 30:11-16); Elkanah lets Hannah's vow stand (verse 23).

decisions.choice: Yahweh of hosts: the title of verse 3, now used in prayer
decisions.reason: Hannah calls on God by the title the narrator introduced in verse 3: the King who commands every power in heaven and on earth. She brings the request of one powerless woman to him.

decisions.choice: look on the affliction ... remember me: what God did for Hagar, Leah and Rachel
decisions.reason: Yahweh heard Hagar's affliction (Genesis 16:11) and saw Leah's affliction (Genesis 29:32), and God remembered Rachel and opened her womb (Genesis 30:22). Hannah asks for the same. "Look indeed" doubles the verb: she pleads with God truly to see. The answer comes in verse 19: Yahweh remembered her.

decisions.choice: your maidservant: a humble way to speak of herself
decisions.reason: 'Amah is a female servant. Hannah calls herself by it three times, as one who depends on her master's kindness (compare Ruth 3:9), and she uses it again to Eli (verse 16).

decisions.choice: seed of men: a male child
decisions.reason: "Seed" means offspring, and "of men" makes it male: she asks for a son.

decisions.choice: no razor on his head: the sign of a Nazirite
decisions.reason: Uncut hair was the sign that a person was set apart to Yahweh under a Nazirite vow (Numbers 6:5). Numbers 6 describes a vow that a man or woman takes for a set time; Hannah gives her son for life, as Samson was set apart from the womb (Judges 13:5, 7). Hannah does not use the word Nazirite here; see m8.

decisions.choice: I will give him to Yahweh all the days of his life: for life, not for a set time
decisions.reason: Levites served from the age of twenty-five or thirty to fifty (Numbers 4:3; 8:24-25), and a Nazirite vow under Numbers 6 lasted a set time. Samuel is to belong to Yahweh as long as he lives (verses 22 and 28). Hannah turns from speaking to Yahweh to speaking about him ("to Yahweh"), as in a formal promise.

decisions.choice: the Hebrew text ends the vow with the razor
alternatives: adds: and he will drink no wine or strong drink (ancient Greek)
decisions.reason: The ancient Greek translation adds after "his head": "and wine and strong drink he will not drink", the other main Nazirite rule (Numbers 6:3). In verse 22 a Hebrew manuscript of Samuel found at Qumran calls Samuel a Nazirite "for ever, all the days of his life". The Masoretic text has neither, and it is followed here; the razor alone already points to the Nazirite vow. Reviewers should check these readings against the textual evidence.

decisions.choice: the LORD of Armies
decisions.reason: As in verse 3.

decisions.choice: servant; a son
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "maidservant" and "a seed of men"; Balanced and Readable say "servant" and "a son" (m4, m5).

decisions.choice: Please see ... remember me. Do not forget me. If you will give me a son ...
decisions.reason: Readable turns the first conditions into plain requests and keeps the "if ... then" form for the heart of the vow: if God gives her a son, she will give him to the LORD. It also says "made a solemn promise" for "vowed a vow" and "No razor will ever cut his hair".

records.source: וְהָיָה֙ כִּ֣י הִרְבְּתָ֔ה לְהִתְפַּלֵּ֖ל לִפְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה וְעֵלִ֖י שֹׁמֵ֥ר אֶת־פִּֽיהָ׃
records.gloss: And it was, as she multiplied to pray before Yahweh, and Eli [was] watching her mouth.
pieces: As she went on praying before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, Eli was watching her mouth.

L.12: And it was, as she kept on praying before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, that Eli was watching her mouth.

R.12: Hannah kept on praying to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} for a long time, and Eli was watching her mouth.

decisions.choice: she multiplied to pray: she prayed on and on
decisions.reason: The verb means to do much or to keep on: her prayer went on at length.

decisions.choice: before Yahweh: at his sanctuary, in his presence
decisions.reason: To pray "before Yahweh" is to pray at the place where he was present with the ark (verses 15 and 19).

decisions.choice: that (Literal); for a long time (Readable)
decisions.reason: Literal adds "that" to join the clauses after "And it was"; Readable spells out what "kept on praying" implies.

records.source: וְחַנָּ֗ה הִ֚יא מְדַבֶּ֣רֶת עַל־לִבָּ֔הּ רַ֚ק שְׂפָתֶ֣יהָ נָּע֔וֹת וְקוֹלָ֖הּ לֹ֣א יִשָּׁמֵ֑עַ וַיַּחְשְׁבֶ֥הָ עֵלִ֖י לְשִׁכֹּרָֽה׃
records.gloss: And Hannah, she [was] speaking on her heart; only her lips [were] moving, and her voice was not heard; and thought her Eli to [be] a drunken [woman].
pieces: Hannah was speaking within herself. Only her lips moved; no sound of her voice could be heard. So Eli thought she was drunk.

L.13: Now Hannah was speaking in her heart; only her lips were moving, and her voice was not heard. And Eli took her to be drunk.

R.13: Hannah was praying silently. Her lips were moving, but no sound came out. So Eli thought she was drunk.

decisions.choice: speaking on her heart: praying silently, within herself
decisions.reason: To speak "on" or "to" one's heart is to speak inwardly (Genesis 24:45, of Abraham's servant praying silently). Prayer was usually spoken aloud (Psalm 3:5), which is why Eli misreads what he sees.

decisions.choice: Eli thought she was drunk
decisions.reason: The feast included wine (verse 9, "after drinking"), and Eli takes her moving lips and silent voice for the mumbling of a woman who has drunk too much.

decisions.choice: speaking within herself (Balanced); praying silently (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of the idiom (m1).

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֵלֶ֨יהָ֙ עֵלִ֔י עַד־מָתַ֖י תִּשְׁתַּכָּרִ֑ין הָסִ֥ירִי אֶת־יֵינֵ֖ךְ מֵעָלָֽיִךְ׃
records.gloss: And said to her Eli, Until when will you make yourself drunk? Put away your wine from upon you.
pieces: Eli said to her, "How long will you go on being drunk? Get rid of your wine!"

L.14: And Eli said to her, "How long will you be drunk? Put away your wine from you."

R.14: Eli said to her, "How long are you going to stay drunk? Stop drinking and get sober!"

decisions.choice: until when: a rebuke
decisions.reason: "Until when?" is a reproach: how long will this go on? (Exodus 10:3; 1 Samuel 16:1).

decisions.choice: put away your wine from you: stop drinking and become sober
decisions.reason: Eli tells her to get rid of the wine that is in her, to sober up, and so also to stop drinking.

decisions.choice: Stop drinking and get sober!
decisions.reason: Readable says what the command means (m2).

records.source: וַתַּ֨עַן חַנָּ֤ה וַתֹּ֨אמֶר֙ לֹ֣א אֲדֹנִ֔י אִשָּׁ֤ה קְשַׁת־ר֨וּחַ֙ אָנֹ֔כִי וְיַ֥יִן וְשֵׁכָ֖ר לֹ֣א שָׁתִ֑יתִי וָאֶשְׁפֹּ֥ךְ אֶת־נַפְשִׁ֖י לִפְנֵ֥י יְהוָֽה׃
records.gloss: And answered Hannah and said, No, my lord, a woman hard of spirit [am] I; and wine and strong drink I have not drunk, and I have poured out my soul before Yahweh.
pieces: But Hannah answered, "No, my lord, I am a woman deeply troubled in spirit. I have not been drinking wine or beer; I have been pouring out my soul before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

L.15: And Hannah answered and said, "No, my lord, I [am] a woman hard of spirit. I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but I have poured out my soul before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

R.15: "No, sir," Hannah answered. "I am a very unhappy woman. I have not been drinking wine or beer. I have been telling {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} all my sorrow.

decisions.choice: my lord: a respectful address to a man
decisions.reason: Hannah speaks to the priest as to a man of higher rank; this is not the title used for God.

decisions.choice: hard of spirit: weighed down with trouble
decisions.reason: The phrase is found only here. "Hard" is used elsewhere of a heavy lot, such as hard labor (Exodus 6:9). Hannah is not light-headed with drink, as Eli thinks, but heavy with grief.

decisions.choice: strong drink: intoxicating drink other than wine
decisions.reason: Shekhar is any intoxicating drink, such as beer made from grain or drink made from other fruit. Wine and strong drink are named together in the Nazirite law (Numbers 6:3) and in the rule for priests on duty (Leviticus 10:9).

decisions.choice: poured out my soul: told Yahweh all her grief
decisions.reason: To pour out one's soul or heart is to empty out everything one feels before God (Psalm 42:5; 62:9; Lamentations 2:19). Hannah has not been pouring drink; she has been pouring out herself.

decisions.choice: beer
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "strong drink"; Balanced and Readable say "beer", as in Numbers 6:3 (m3).

decisions.choice: sir; a very unhappy woman; telling the LORD all my sorrow
decisions.reason: Readable uses the everyday polite address and gives the sense of the two idioms (m2, m4).

records.source: אַל־תִּתֵּן֙ אֶת־אֲמָ֣תְךָ֔ לִפְנֵ֖י בַּת־בְּלִיָּ֑עַל כִּֽי־מֵרֹ֥ב שִׂיחִ֛י וְכַעְסִ֖י דִּבַּ֥רְתִּי עַד־הֵֽנָּה׃
records.gloss: Do not give your maidservant before [the] face of a daughter of worthlessness, for from [the] abundance of my complaint and my provocation I have spoken until now.
pieces: Do not take your servant for a worthless woman. All this time I have been speaking out of my great anguish and distress."

L.16: Do not regard your maidservant as a daughter of worthlessness, for out of the abundance of my complaint and my provocation I have spoken until now."

R.16: Please do not think I am a wicked woman. I have been praying here so long because I am so troubled and hurt."

decisions.choice: do not give your maidservant before a daughter of worthlessness: do not take me for a worthless woman
decisions.reason: "Daughter of" describes character: a "daughter of belial" is a woman of no worth, a disgrace. The same word is used of Eli's own sons, "sons of belial" (2:12).

decisions.choice: my complaint: troubled thoughts poured out in words
decisions.reason: Siach is anxious thinking and the outpouring of it in words, often in prayer (Psalm 142:3; Job 7:13).

decisions.choice: my provocation: the grief of being provoked
decisions.reason: It is the same word as in verses 6 and 7: what Peninnah's taunts have done to her.

decisions.choice: anguish and distress (Balanced); so troubled and hurt (Readable)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "complaint" and "provocation"; Balanced and Readable give their sense (m2, m3). Readable adds "here so long" for "until now".

records.source: וַיַּ֧עַן עֵלִ֛י וַיֹּ֖אמֶר לְכִ֣י לְשָׁל֑וֹם וֵאלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל יִתֵּן֙ אֶת־שֵׁ֣לָתֵ֔ךְ אֲשֶׁ֥ר שָׁאַ֖לְתְּ מֵעִמּֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And answered Eli and said, Go in peace, and [the] God of Israel grant your petition which you have asked from with him.
pieces: Eli answered, "Go in peace. May the God of Israel grant what you have asked of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}."

L.17: And Eli answered and said, "Go in peace, and may the God of Israel grant your petition that you have asked of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}."

R.17: Then Eli said, "Go in peace. May the God of Israel give you what you have asked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} for."

decisions.choice: may he grant: a blessing
alternatives: the God of Israel will grant
decisions.reason: The verb can be read as a wish, "may he grant", or as a promise, "he will grant". Spoken by the priest as he sends her away, it is a blessing, and Hannah receives it with hope (verse 18).

decisions.choice: your petition that you asked: the key word of the story
decisions.reason: The noun and the verb come from sha'al, "to ask". The word returns when Hannah names her son (verse 20) and when she gives him to Yahweh (verses 27-28), and it sounds like the name Saul, sha'ul, "asked for", the king whom Israel will ask for (8:10; 12:13).

decisions.choice: Go in peace: a farewell blessing
decisions.reason: Shalom is wholeness and well-being. The words send her away with good wishes (Judges 18:6; 2 Kings 5:19).

records.source: וַתֹּ֕אמֶר תִּמְצָ֧א שִׁפְחָתְךָ֛ חֵ֖ן בְּעֵינֶ֑יךָ וַתֵּ֨לֶךְ הָאִשָּׁ֤ה לְדַרְכָּהּ֙ וַתֹּאכַ֔ל וּפָנֶ֥יהָ לֹא־הָיוּ־לָ֖הּ עֽוֹד׃
records.gloss: And she said, May find your maidservant favor in your eyes. And went the woman on her way, and she ate, and her face was not to her anymore.
pieces: She said, "May your servant find favor in your sight." Then the woman went her way and ate, and her face was no longer downcast.

L.18: And she said, "May your maidservant find favor in your eyes." And the woman went on her way and ate, and her face was no longer [sad].

R.18: Hannah answered, "Thank you, sir. I hope you will always think well of me." Then she went away and ate something, and she no longer looked sad.

decisions.choice: your maidservant: a humbler word
decisions.reason: Here she uses shifchah, a humbler word for a servant girl than the 'amah of verses 11 and 16 (compare Ruth 2:13). She answers the priest with thanks and respect.

decisions.choice: find favor in your eyes: may you think kindly of me
decisions.reason: This is a polite way to thank someone or to ask that they stay kind (Genesis 33:15; Ruth 2:13).

decisions.choice: her face was no longer hers: she no longer looked sad
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "her face was not to her anymore", a short expression whose sense is clear from the story: the downcast face of verses 7-8 was gone. The ancient Greek reads "her face did not fall anymore". Hannah ate the meal she had refused (verse 7), because her grief had lifted.

decisions.choice: her face was no longer [sad]
decisions.reason: Literal supplies the word the short Hebrew expression implies (m3).

decisions.choice: Thank you, sir. I hope you will always think well of me.
decisions.reason: Readable gives the sense of the polite formula (m2) and puts Hannah's words in the first person.

records.source: וַיַּשְׁכִּ֣מוּ בַבֹּ֗קֶר וַיִּֽשְׁתַּחֲווּ֙ לִפְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה וַיָּשֻׁ֛בוּ וַיָּבֹ֥אוּ אֶל־בֵּיתָ֖ם הָרָמָ֑תָה וַיֵּ֤דַע אֶלְקָנָה֙ אֶת־חַנָּ֣ה אִשְׁתּ֔וֹ וַיִּֽזְכְּרֶ֖הָ יְהוָֽה׃
records.gloss: And they rose early in the morning and bowed down before Yahweh, and they returned and came to their house, to Ramah. And knew Elkanah Hannah his wife, and remembered her Yahweh.
pieces: Early the next morning they worshiped before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and then went back home to Ramah. Elkanah lay with his wife Hannah, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} remembered her.

L.19: And they rose early in the morning and worshiped before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and they returned and came to their house at Ramah. And Elkanah knew Hannah his wife, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} remembered her.

R.19: Early the next morning the family worshiped {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. Then they went back home to Ramah. Elkanah slept with his wife Hannah, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} remembered her and answered her prayer.

decisions.choice: Ramah: the town of verse 1
decisions.reason: Ramah, "the height", is the short name of Ramathaim-zophim (verse 1). It stays Samuel's home all his life (7:17; 25:1).

decisions.choice: knew: had sexual relations with
decisions.reason: To "know" one's wife is a gentle way of speaking of married love (Genesis 4:1).

decisions.choice: Yahweh remembered her: he acted on her behalf
decisions.reason: When God "remembers" someone, he does not recall what he had forgotten; he turns to act for them, as he remembered Noah (Genesis 8:1) and Rachel (Genesis 30:22). Hannah had asked him to remember her (verse 11).

decisions.choice: lay with (Balanced); slept with ... and answered her prayer (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use plain words for "knew" (m2). Readable adds what Yahweh's remembering meant for Hannah (m3).

records.source: וַיְהִי֙ לִתְקֻפ֣וֹת הַיָּמִ֔ים וַתַּ֥הַר חַנָּ֖ה וַתֵּ֣לֶד בֵּ֑ן וַתִּקְרָ֤א אֶת־שְׁמוֹ֙ שְׁמוּאֵ֔ל כִּ֥י מֵיְהוָ֖ה שְׁאִלְתִּֽיו׃
records.gloss: And it was at [the] turnings of the days, and conceived Hannah and bore a son, and she called his name Samuel, for from Yahweh I asked him.
pieces: In due time Hannah became pregnant and bore a son. She called him Samuel, for she said,"I asked {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} for him."

L.20: And it was at the turning of the days [that] Hannah conceived and bore a son, and she called his name Samuel, for [she said], "From {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} I asked him."

R.20: Hannah became pregnant, and when the time came she had a son. She named him Samuel. She said, "I asked {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} for him."

decisions.choice: at the turning of the days: when the time came round
alternatives: at the turn of the year
decisions.reason: The phrase is used of the turn of the year (Exodus 34:22; 2 Chronicles 24:23). It may mean that by the next yearly visit Hannah had her son, or simply that she gave birth when the time of her pregnancy was complete. Either way the child came in God's time.

decisions.choice: Samuel: a name explained by "asked"
decisions.reason: The name Samuel, Shemu'el, most likely means "name of God" (some hear in it "heard by God"). Hannah's explanation, "from Yahweh I asked him", is a play on sound rather than a definition: the verb sha'al, "ask", echoes in the name. Scripture often gives a name its meaning from the story of a birth (Genesis 29:32-35). The same verb sounds even more like Saul, sha'ul, "asked for" (see verse 17).

decisions.choice: for from Yahweh I asked him: Hannah's own words
decisions.reason: The sentence switches to "I", so these are the words Hannah said as she named him.

decisions.choice: for [she said] (Literal); for she said (Balanced); She said (Readable)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew moves straight into Hannah's words without "she said"; every level supplies it so the reader knows who speaks (m3).

records.source: וַיַּ֛עַל הָאִ֥ישׁ אֶלְקָנָ֖ה וְכָל־בֵּית֑וֹ לִזְבֹּ֧חַ לַֽיהוָ֛ה אֶת־זֶ֥בַח הַיָּמִ֖ים וְאֶת־נִדְרֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And went up the man Elkanah and all his house to sacrifice to Yahweh the sacrifice of the days and his vow.
pieces: Elkanah went up with his whole household to offer {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} the yearly sacrifice and to pay his vow.

L.21: And the man Elkanah and all his house went up to sacrifice to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} the yearly sacrifice and his vow.

R.21: Once again Elkanah went up with all his family to offer the yearly sacrifice to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and to keep his vow.

decisions.choice: the sacrifice of the days: the yearly sacrifice
decisions.reason: "Days" means a year, as in verse 3.

decisions.choice: his vow: a vow of Elkanah's own, or his share in Hannah's vow
decisions.reason: The story has not mentioned a vow of Elkanah's. He may have made one of his own, perhaps in thanks for the son. Or "his vow" may be Hannah's vow, which he had let stand as her husband and so made his own (Numbers 30:11-16). A vow was often paid with a sacrifice (Leviticus 7:16; Deuteronomy 12:6).

decisions.choice: to pay his vow (Balanced); to keep his vow (Readable)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew joins "his vow" to the verb "sacrifice"; Balanced and Readable supply a verb that fits a vow. Readable adds "Once again" to show that this is the next yearly visit.

records.source: וְחַנָּ֖ה לֹ֣א עָלָ֑תָה כִּֽי־אָמְרָ֣ה לְאִישָׁ֗הּ עַ֣ד יִגָּמֵ֤ל הַנַּ֨עַר֙ וַהֲבִאֹתִ֗יו וְנִרְאָה֙ אֶת־פְּנֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה וְיָ֥שַׁב שָׁ֖ם עַד־עוֹלָֽם׃
records.gloss: And Hannah did not go up, for she said to her husband, Until is weaned the boy; and I will bring him, and he will appear [before the] face of Yahweh and dwell there until forever.
pieces: But Hannah did not go. She told her husband, "Once the boy is weaned, I will bring him to appear before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and he will stay there for the rest of his life."

L.22: But Hannah did not go up, for she said to her husband, "[Not] until the boy is weaned; then I will bring him, and he will appear before the face of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and dwell there forever."

R.22: But Hannah stayed home. She told her husband, "When the boy no longer needs to nurse, I will take him to Shiloh. He will be presented to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and live there for the rest of his life."

decisions.choice: weaned: perhaps two or three years old
decisions.reason: Children were nursed much longer than is usual today, often for two or three years, and a feast could mark the weaning (Genesis 21:8). Samuel would still be a small child when he came to Shiloh (verse 24), but old enough to be cared for by others and to serve (2:11, 18).

decisions.choice: appear before Yahweh: be presented at his sanctuary
decisions.reason: The phrase is used of Israel's men appearing before Yahweh at the yearly feasts (Exodus 23:17; 34:23; Deuteronomy 16:16). Samuel will appear there not for a feast but to stay.

decisions.choice: until forever: for good, all his life
decisions.reason: "Until forever" here means permanently, for the whole of his life, as Hannah vowed (verse 11) and says again in verse 28.

decisions.choice: [Not] until
decisions.reason: Hannah's words begin with "until", leaving "I will not go up" to be understood from the start of the verse; Literal supplies "Not".

decisions.choice: stayed home; no longer needs to nurse; to Shiloh
decisions.reason: Readable explains "weaned" and names the place where the LORD's house was (verse 3).

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לָהּ֩ אֶלְקָנָ֨ה אִישָׁ֜הּ עֲשִׂ֧י הַטּ֣וֹב בְּעֵינַ֗יִךְ שְׁבִי֙ עַד־גָּמְלֵ֣ךְ אֹת֔וֹ אַ֛ךְ יָקֵ֥ם יְהוָ֖ה אֶת־דְּבָר֑וֹ וַתֵּ֤שֶׁב הָֽאִשָּׁה֙ וַתֵּ֣ינֶק אֶת־בְּנָ֔הּ עַד־גָּמְלָ֖הּ אֹתֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And said to her Elkanah her husband, Do the good in your eyes; stay until you have weaned him; only may establish Yahweh his word. And stayed the woman and nursed her son until she weaned him.
pieces: Her husband Elkanah told her, "Do what seems best to you. Stay at home until you have weaned him. Only may {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} make {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} word come true." So the woman stayed home and nursed her son until she had weaned him.

L.23: And Elkanah her husband said to her, "Do what [is] good in your eyes; stay until you have weaned him; only may {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} establish {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} word." So the woman stayed and nursed her son until she weaned him.

R.23: Her husband Elkanah said to her, "Do whatever you think is best. Stay here until he no longer needs to nurse. I only pray that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will do what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has said." So Hannah stayed home and nursed her son until he was old enough to stop.

decisions.choice: Do what is good in your eyes: Elkanah agrees to her plan
decisions.reason: As her husband he could have cancelled her vow (Numbers 30:11-16). Instead he lets her decide when to bring the boy, and so he confirms the vow.

decisions.choice: may Yahweh establish his word: the Hebrew text
alternatives: may Yahweh establish what has gone out of your mouth (ancient Greek, Qumran)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew text reads "his word", meaning Yahweh's. No word of Yahweh about the boy has been reported; it may mean Eli's blessing taken as Yahweh's promise (verse 17), or Yahweh's purpose in giving the child. The ancient Greek translation and a Hebrew manuscript from Qumran read "what has gone out of your mouth", that is, may Yahweh help Hannah to keep her vow. The Hebrew text is followed here; reviewers should check the readings.

decisions.choice: make his word come true (Balanced); do what he has said (Readable); Hannah
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what it means for the LORD to "establish" a word. Readable names Hannah for "the woman" and explains "weaned".

records.source: וַתַּעֲלֵ֨הוּ עִמָּ֜הּ כַּאֲשֶׁ֣ר גְּמָלַ֗תּוּ בְּפָרִ֤ים שְׁלֹשָׁה֙ וְאֵיפָ֨ה אַחַ֥ת קֶ֨מַח֙ וְנֵ֣בֶל יַ֔יִן וַתְּבִאֵ֥הוּ בֵית־יְהוָ֖ה שִׁל֑וֹ וְהַנַּ֖עַר נָֽעַר׃
records.gloss: And she brought him up with her when she had weaned him, with three bulls and one ephah of flour and a skin of wine, and brought him [to the] house of Yahweh [at] Shiloh; and the boy [was] a boy.
pieces: Once she had weaned him, she took him up with her, along with three bulls, {{units:about 20 quarts|an ephah}} of flour and a skin of wine, and brought him to the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} at Shiloh. The boy was still young.

L.24: And she brought him up with her when she had weaned him, with three bulls, and one ephah of flour, and a skin of wine, and she brought him to the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} [at] Shiloh; and the boy [was] young.

R.24: When Samuel was weaned, Hannah took him with her to the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} at Shiloh. She also took three bulls, {{units:about 20 quarts|an ephah}} of flour, and a leather bag of wine. Samuel was still very young.

decisions.choice: three bulls: the Hebrew text
decisions.reason: The Hebrew text has "three bulls", but verse 25 speaks of "the bull". The ancient Greek translation and a Hebrew manuscript from Qumran read "a bull three years old", which differs only slightly in the Hebrew letters and fits verse 25. With three bulls, "the bull" of verse 25 is the one offered when the boy was presented. The Hebrew text is followed here.

decisions.choice: an ephah of flour and a skin of wine: a generous offering
decisions.reason: An ephah was about 20 quarts. Flour and wine went with a bull offered as a sacrifice (Numbers 15:8-10 asks three tenths of an ephah of flour and half a hin of wine for each bull); Hannah brings far more. The word for the wine container can mean a leather skin or a large clay jar (Jeremiah 13:12).

decisions.choice: the boy was a boy: the child was still young
decisions.reason: Repeating the word stresses how young he was: a little child, just weaned, given to the sanctuary.

decisions.choice: Samuel; a leather bag of wine
decisions.reason: Readable names Samuel and Hannah for "him" and "she", and says what a skin was.

records.source: וַֽיִּשְׁחֲט֖וּ אֶת־הַפָּ֑ר וַיָּבִ֥יאוּ אֶת־הַנַּ֖עַר אֶל־עֵלִֽי׃
records.gloss: And they slaughtered the bull, and they brought the boy to Eli.
pieces: They slaughtered the bull and brought the boy to Eli.

L.25: And they slaughtered the bull, and they brought the boy to Eli.

R.25: After they had killed the bull as a sacrifice, they brought the boy to Eli.

decisions.choice: slaughtered the bull: the sacrifice that marked the boy's presentation
decisions.reason: The bull was killed as an offering, probably a burnt offering given wholly to Yahweh (Leviticus 1:3-5), as Samuel himself was being given wholly to him. On the number of bulls, see verse 24.

decisions.choice: as a sacrifice
decisions.reason: Readable says why the bull was killed.

records.source: וַתֹּ֨אמֶר֙ בִּ֣י אֲדֹנִ֔י חֵ֥י נַפְשְׁךָ֖ אֲדֹנִ֑י אֲנִ֣י הָאִשָּׁ֗ה הַנִּצֶּ֤בֶת עִמְּכָה֙ בָּזֶ֔ה לְהִתְפַּלֵּ֖ל אֶל־יְהוָֽה׃
records.gloss: And she said, Please, my lord, [by the] life of your soul, my lord, I [am] the woman standing with you in this [place] to pray to Yahweh.
pieces: Hannah said, "Pardon me, my lord! As surely as you live, my lord, I am the woman who once stood beside you here, praying to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

L.26: And she said, "Please, my lord! [As] your soul lives, my lord, I [am] the woman who stood beside you here, praying to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

R.26: Hannah said to Eli, "Excuse me, sir. I promise you, I am the woman who stood here next to you and prayed to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: please, my lord: asking leave to speak
decisions.reason: Bi, "please" or "pardon me", is how one asks a superior to listen (Genesis 43:20; Judges 6:13).

decisions.choice: as your soul lives: an oath, "as surely as you live"
decisions.reason: Swearing by a person's life was a solemn way to assure them that what follows is true (17:55; 20:3; 25:26). Some years have passed, and Hannah assures Eli that she is the woman he saw.

decisions.choice: the woman who stood beside you here: the scene of verses 9-18
decisions.reason: Hannah points back to the place and the prayer that Eli saw, so that he will see what Yahweh has done.

decisions.choice: Excuse me, sir. I promise you
decisions.reason: Readable uses an everyday polite address and gives the sense of the oath (m2). It names Eli as the one she speaks to.

records.source: אֶל־הַנַּ֥עַר הַזֶּ֖ה הִתְפַּלָּ֑לְתִּי וַיִּתֵּ֨ן יְהוָ֥ה לִי֙ אֶת־שְׁאֵ֣לָתִ֔י אֲשֶׁ֥ר שָׁאַ֖לְתִּי מֵעִמּֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: For the boy, this [one], I prayed, and gave Yahweh to me my petition which I asked from with him.
pieces: I prayed for this boy, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has granted me what I asked of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

L.27: For this boy I prayed, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has given me my petition that I asked of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.27: I prayed for this boy, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has given me what I asked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} for.

decisions.choice: for this boy I prayed: the boy comes first
decisions.reason: The sentence begins with "for this boy", pointing to the child in front of them: here is the answer to the prayer Eli saw.

decisions.choice: my petition that I asked: the words of Eli's blessing
decisions.reason: Eli's blessing used the same words: "may the God of Israel grant your petition that you have asked of him" (verse 17). Hannah shows him that it has come true.

records.source: וְגַ֣ם אָנֹכִ֗י הִשְׁאִלְתִּ֨הוּ֙ לַֽיהוָ֔ה כָּל־הַיָּמִים֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר הָיָ֔ה ה֥וּא שָׁא֖וּל לַֽיהוָ֑ה וַיִּשְׁתַּ֥חוּ שָׁ֖ם לַיהוָֽה׃פ
records.gloss: And also I have granted him to Yahweh; all the days which he is, he [is] asked for Yahweh. And he bowed down there to Yahweh.
pieces: So I in turn give him to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. All the days of his life he is given over to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}." And he worshiped {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} there.

L.28: And I in turn have granted him to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}; all the days that he lives, he [is] granted to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}." And he worshiped {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} there.

R.28: Now I am giving him to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. For his whole life he will belong to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}." And he worshiped {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} there.

decisions.choice: granted him ... granted: handed over in answer to asking
decisions.reason: The verb is sha'al again, "ask", in a form that means to let someone have what was asked, to grant or hand over (Exodus 12:36 uses it of the Egyptians giving Israel what it asked). It is not a loan to be taken back: the boy belongs to Yahweh "all the days that he lives". Hannah asked Yahweh for him, and now she gives him to Yahweh as one "asked", sha'ul, a word that sounds like the name Saul.

decisions.choice: I in turn: Hannah answers Yahweh's gift with her own
decisions.reason: "And also I" sets Hannah's act beside Yahweh's: he gave her what she asked (verse 27), and she in turn gives the boy to him.

decisions.choice: he worshiped there: Elkanah, or the boy Samuel
decisions.reason: The verb is singular, "he bowed down". It may refer to Elkanah, the head of the family, or to the young Samuel, whose life before Yahweh begins here. Some Hebrew manuscripts and the ancient Latin translation read "they worshiped".

decisions.choice: granted (Literal); give, given over (Balanced); giving, belong (Readable)
decisions.reason: Familiar English versions say "lent", which keeps the repeated word but suggests a loan to be returned. Literal says "granted" twice, which keeps the repeated word with the right sense; Balanced and Readable say what the verb means (m1).
